items.stem: A company plans to launch six Amazon EC2 instances of one instance type in a single Availability Zone for a new application. The instances will be launched together from one launch template, and the application team manages them. The instances exchange data constantly, and the application needs low latency and high throughput between them. Which placement approach for the instances will meet these requirements?
keywords: low latency and high throughput between them

options.text: Launch all six instances into a cluster placement group in the Availability Zone.
options.why: AWS recommends a cluster placement group for [low network latency, high network throughput, or both](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-placement-cluster-recommended-traffic-between-instances) when most traffic stays [between the instances in the group](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-placement-cluster-recommended-traffic-between-instances).

options.text: Launch all six instances into a spread placement group in the Availability Zone.
options.why: A spread placement group keeps the instances [each placed on distinct hardware](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-placement-spread-critical-instances), which protects against shared failures but does not bring them closer together.
options.misconception: distinct hardware also gives low latency between instances

options.text: Launch the instances into a partition placement group with two partitions of three instances each.
options.why: Each partition [has its own set of racks](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-placement-partition-separate-racks) to [isolate the impact of hardware failure](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-placement-partition-separate-racks), not to bring the instances close together.
options.misconception: partitions place instances close together for speed

options.text: Launch the instances without a placement group, and let Amazon EC2 spread them across the underlying hardware.
options.why: Without a group, Amazon EC2 keeps instances [spread out across the underlying hardware](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-placement-optional-default-spread-out) to limit correlated failures, which works against low latency between them.
options.misconception: the default placement already gives the best network between instances

items.explanation: Traffic between the instances decides this question. A cluster placement group places the instances close together for [low network latency, high network throughput, or both](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-placement-cluster-recommended-traffic-between-instances). A cluster placement group [can't span multiple Availability Zones](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-placement-cluster-single-az), which fits six instances in a single zone.
items.takeaway: Traffic between the instances means a cluster placement group; separate hardware for a few critical instances means a spread placement group.
items.twin: If the stem said "The instances are mission-critical, and one hardware failure must not affect more than one of them" instead: a spread placement group, with instances [each placed on distinct hardware](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-placement-spread-critical-instances).
items.say: The instances talk to each other all the time, so I'd put them in a cluster placement group.

solvers.stem_only: Put all six instances in a cluster placement group in the one Availability Zone for low latency and high throughput between them.

items.stem: A company runs a licensed application on one Amazon EC2 instance in a private subnet. Partner systems allow-list the private IP address of the application, and the software license is bound to the MAC address that the application uses. A hot standby instance with the same software runs in the same Availability Zone. If the primary instance fails, traffic must move to the standby with minimal downtime and without DNS or route table changes. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
keywords: without DNS or route table changes

options.text: Give the application its address on a secondary network interface, and attach that interface to a standby instance in another Availability Zone after a failure.
options.why: A network interface attaches to instances [in the same Availability Zone](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-eni-attributes-follow-same-az), so it cannot move to a standby in another zone.

options.text: Detach the primary network interface from the failed instance, and attach it to the standby instance so that its addresses and MAC address move.
options.why: [You can't detach a primary network interface](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-eni-primary-cannot-detach), so the addresses on the primary interface stay with the failed instance.
options.misconception: the primary network interface moves like a secondary one

options.text: Give the application its address on a secondary network interface, and attach that interface to the standby instance in the same zone after a failure.
options.why: The interface [maintains its private IP addresses, Elastic IP addresses](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-eni-hot-standby-failover) and its MAC address, so traffic reaches the standby with [no changes to the route table](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-eni-hot-standby-failover).

options.text: Launch a replacement instance from a recent AMI after a failure, assign it the same private IP address, and register its new MAC address with the vendor.
options.why: A new launch works, but each failure then needs an image, a launch and a license change, which is more downtime and more work than moving an interface.

items.explanation: The addresses and the MAC address have to move without DNS changes, and a secondary network interface does that. [The attributes of a network interface follow it](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-eni-attributes-follow-same-az) to the new instance, and [network traffic is redirected](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-eni-attributes-follow-same-az). The move works because the standby is [in the same Availability Zone](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-eni-attributes-follow-same-az).
items.takeaway: To fail over at the same private IP address and MAC address, move a secondary network interface to a standby in the same zone.
items.twin: If the stem said "the standby instance runs in another Availability Zone" instead: moving the interface fails, because a network interface attaches to instances [in the same Availability Zone](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-eni-attributes-follow-same-az).
items.say: I'd keep the address on a secondary network interface and move it to the standby in the same zone.

solvers.stem_only: Put the application address on a secondary network interface (ENI) and move that interface to the standby instance in the same Availability Zone; the private IP and MAC address move with it. A primary interface cannot be detached, and an ENI cannot cross Availability Zones.

items.stem: A company runs an analytics service on Amazon EC2 general purpose instances. The service loads a large data set into memory and runs queries against it. During busy periods, the service runs out of memory and slows down, but CPU utilization stays below 30%. Disk activity on the instances is low. The company wants to change the instance family without changing the application. Which instance family meets these requirements?
keywords: Disk activity on the instances is low

options.text: Compute optimized instances, such as the C family, with more vCPUs for each instance
options.why: Compute optimized instances serve [compute intensive applications](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-family-compute-optimized), and CPU stays low here, so more vCPUs do not fix the memory shortage.
options.misconception: more CPU fixes any slow application

options.text: Burstable performance instances, such as the T family, that earn credits for the busy periods
options.why: A burstable instance [spends credits when it bursts above the baseline](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-burstable-standard-earn-spend-credits) of CPU, and CPU credits add no memory.
options.misconception: burst credits also cover memory peaks

options.text: Storage optimized instances, such as the I family, with fast local storage for the data set
options.why: Storage optimized instances serve [very large data sets on local storage](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-family-storage-optimized) with heavy disk access, and disk activity here is low.
options.misconception: a large data set needs storage optimized instances

options.text: Memory optimized instances, such as the R family, with enough memory for the data set
options.why: Memory optimized instances [deliver fast performance](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-family-memory-optimized) for workloads that [process large data sets in memory](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-family-memory-optimized), and memory is the limit here.

items.explanation: Find the resource that runs out. Here it is memory, and CPU and disk stay low. Memory optimized instances are built for workloads that [process large data sets in memory](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-family-memory-optimized). In an instance type name, the letter R stands for [memory optimized](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-instance-type-series-letters).
items.takeaway: Match the instance family to the resource that runs out: memory points to R, CPU to C, local disk to I.
items.twin: If the stem said "CPU utilization stays above 90% and memory use is low" instead: compute optimized instances, because they serve [compute intensive applications](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-family-compute-optimized).
items.say: Memory is what runs out, so I'd move to a memory optimized R instance.

solvers.stem_only: Memory-bound with low CPU and disk use: move to a memory optimized family (R or X) with enough memory for the data set.

items.stem: A company runs Amazon EC2 instances in private subnets. Administrators connect to the instances with SSH through a bastion host in a public subnet. A security review asks the company to restrict administrator access: the instances must have no inbound ports open, and the company wants to stop managing SSH keys. The instances run the SSM Agent and already reach the AWS service endpoints that they need. Which combination of steps will meet these requirements in the MOST secure way? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Attach an IAM role with the AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore managed policy to each instance through an instance profile.
options.why: Session Manager connects when the instance has an attached IAM role with the [AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-session-manager-prereq-iam-role) policy, and the role gives the agent temporary credentials.

options.text: Keep the bastion host, and rotate the SSH keys on the bastion host and on the instances every 30 days.
options.why: Rotation keeps the bastion host and the SSH keys, although Session Manager removes the need to [maintain bastion hosts, or manage SSH keys](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-session-manager-no-inbound-ports-bastion-keys).

options.text: Remove the inbound SSH rules from the instance security groups, and connect to the instances with Session Manager.
options.why: Session Manager works [without the need to open inbound ports](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-session-manager-no-inbound-ports-bastion-keys), so the SSH rules and the bastion host are no longer needed.

options.text: Store the access key of an IAM user on each instance so that the SSM Agent can call Systems Manager.
options.why: It works, but access keys [remain valid until you manually revoke them](../facts/iam.md#iam-long-term-keys-valid-until-revoked-temporary-expire), and the instance role already gives temporary credentials.

options.text: Remove the bastion host, and allow inbound SSH on the instances from the IP address range of the office.
options.why: A narrow source range still leaves the SSH port open and keeps the keys, although Session Manager works [without the need to open inbound ports](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-session-manager-no-inbound-ports-bastion-keys).
options.misconception: a narrow source range makes an open SSH port acceptable

items.explanation: Session Manager meets both requirements. It gives a shell [without the need to open inbound ports](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-session-manager-no-inbound-ports-bastion-keys) and with no SSH keys, and it connects when the instance role has the [AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-session-manager-prereq-iam-role) policy. One step adds the role, and the other step removes the SSH rules.
items.takeaway: No inbound port and no SSH keys means Session Manager plus an instance role with AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore.
items.twin: If the stem said "administrators must keep their own SSH clients, with no bastion host and no public IP addresses" instead: an EC2 Instance Connect Endpoint, which connects [without using a bastion host](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-eice-no-public-ip-no-igw-no-bastion).
items.say: I'd attach a role with the Session Manager policy and close the SSH port.

solvers.stem_only: Use Systems Manager Session Manager: give each instance an IAM role with AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore through an instance profile, then remove the inbound SSH rules (and the bastion) and connect with Session Manager.

items.stem: A company runs a legacy application on one Amazon EC2 instance. The instance is backed by Amazon EBS and uses an x86 instance type. The application cannot run on more than one instance at a time, and it now needs twice its current memory. The company has a 30-minute maintenance window tonight and wants minimal downtime. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
keywords: cannot run on more than one instance

options.text: During the window, change the instance type of the running instance to a larger memory optimized x86 type without stopping it.
options.why: [You must stop your instance](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-resize-must-stop-instance) [before you can change its instance type](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-resize-must-stop-instance), so a running instance keeps its current type.

options.text: During the window, hibernate the instance, change its instance type to a larger memory optimized x86 type, and then resume it.
options.why: After an [instance is hibernated, you can't modify it](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-hibernate-cannot-modify-while-hibernated), so the type change fails.
options.misconception: a hibernated instance can be modified like a stopped one

options.text: Create an AMI of the instance, launch a larger memory optimized x86 instance from the AMI, and point the clients to it.
options.why: A new instance from an AMI works, but it adds an image, a launch and a client change, which is more work than a stop and a type change.

options.text: During the window, stop the instance, change its instance type to a larger memory optimized x86 type, and start it again.
options.why: A stopped instance lets you [modify certain attributes of the instance](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-stopped-instance-type-change), [including the instance type](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-stopped-instance-type-change), and an x86 type keeps [the same processor architecture](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-resize-same-processor-architecture).

items.explanation: Scaling up needs a stop. [You must stop your instance](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-resize-must-stop-instance) [before you can change its instance type](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-resize-must-stop-instance), so you [plan for downtime](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-resize-must-stop-instance) inside the window. The new type keeps [the same processor architecture](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-resize-same-processor-architecture), because the AMI of the instance is built for x86.
items.takeaway: Changing an instance type needs a stop, so plan the stop inside a maintenance window.
items.twin: If the stem said "the application can run on several instances behind a load balancer" instead: add instances, because horizontal scaling means [adding more instances to handle the load](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-compute-guide-vertical-vs-horizontal-definition).
items.say: I'd stop it in the window, change the type to a bigger memory optimized one, and start it again.

steps: I read the last sentence first: it asks for the solution with the LEAST operational overhead that still keeps the downtime minimal.
I mark the constraints: one EBS-backed x86 instance, the application cannot run on two instances, it needs twice the memory, and the maintenance window is 30 minutes tonight.
Before I look at the options, I predict that I change the instance type while the instance runs, because that seems to give zero downtime.
I remove the AMI and new instance option, because it works but adds an image, a launch and a client change. I remove the hibernation option, because a hibernated instance cannot be modified.

Between the change while running and the stop, change and start, the difference is the stop. My first idea breaks because I must stop an EBS-backed instance before I can change its instance type. The stem gives a maintenance window, so a short stop is acceptable.
Check: stop, change to a larger memory optimized x86 type, and start again meets every constraint and keeps the same processor architecture. Time: 90 seconds.

solvers.stem_only: Stop the EBS-backed instance in the window, change the instance type to a larger x86 type with twice the memory, and start it again; same instance, no new endpoint.

items.stem: A company plans to launch six Amazon EC2 instances of one instance type in a single Availability Zone for a new application. The instances will be launched together from one launch template, and the application team manages them. The instances are mission-critical, and one hardware failure must not affect more than one of them. Which placement approach for the instances will meet these requirements?
keywords: one hardware failure must not affect more than one of them

options.text: Launch all six instances into a cluster placement group in the Availability Zone.
options.why: A cluster placement group packs the instances close together for [low network latency, high network throughput, or both](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-placement-cluster-recommended-traffic-between-instances), so one hardware failure can affect several of them.

options.text: Launch all six instances into a spread placement group in the Availability Zone.
options.why: A spread placement group keeps the instances [each placed on distinct hardware](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-placement-spread-critical-instances), and it [reduces the risk of simultaneous failures](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-placement-spread-critical-instances).

options.text: Launch the instances into a partition placement group with two partitions of three instances each.
options.why: Three instances share each partition, and each partition [has its own set of racks](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-placement-partition-separate-racks), so one rack failure can affect several instances of the same partition.
options.misconception: a partition gives each instance its own hardware

options.text: Launch the instances without a placement group, and let Amazon EC2 spread them across the underlying hardware.
options.why: Without a group, Amazon EC2 tries to keep instances [spread out across the underlying hardware](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-placement-optional-default-spread-out), but nothing guarantees distinct hardware for each instance.
options.misconception: the default placement guarantees distinct hardware

items.explanation: The phrase about one hardware failure decides it. A spread placement group is for [a small number of critical instances](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-placement-spread-critical-instances), each on its own hardware. It supports [seven running instances in each Availability Zone](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-placement-spread-max-7-running-per-az), so six instances fit in one zone.
items.takeaway: Separate hardware for a few critical instances means a spread placement group, not a cluster placement group.
items.twin: If the stem said "The instances exchange data constantly, and the application needs low latency and high throughput between them" instead: a cluster placement group, for [low network latency, high network throughput, or both](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-placement-cluster-recommended-traffic-between-instances).
items.say: Each instance has to sit on different hardware, so I'd use a spread placement group.

solvers.stem_only: Use a spread placement group in the Availability Zone: each instance on distinct hardware (six fits within the per-AZ limit of a spread group).

items.stem: A company packages a nightly data export job as a container image. The job runs once each day. Each run is long-running and takes between 2 and 3 hours. The job needs no inbound network access. The operations team is small and prefers a serverless solution, so that nobody patches or scales instances for this job. Which compute options will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Package the job as an AWS Lambda function from the container image, and invoke the function once each day from an Amazon EventBridge schedule.
options.why: A Lambda function runs for at most [15 minutes](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-faq-timeout-15-minutes) per execution, so a run of 2 to 3 hours stops before it finishes.

options.text: Run the container image as an Amazon ECS task on AWS Fargate, and start the task once each day from an Amazon EventBridge schedule.
options.why: Fargate can [run containers without having to manage servers](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-compute-guide-fargate-no-servers-for-containers), and it suits [specific resource needs or persistent processes](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-choose-fargate-containers-persistent) such as a long run.

options.text: Run the container on an Amazon EC2 instance that runs all day, and start the job once each day from a cron entry on the instance.
options.why: It works, but the team patches and scales the instance, an overhead that fits a need for [granular control over the compute environment](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-compute-guide-ec2-overhead-justified-for-control).
options.misconception: keeps an instance running all day for one daily job

options.text: Submit the container image as a daily job to AWS Batch, with a compute environment that uses AWS Fargate resources.
options.why: AWS Batch [automatically provisions compute resources](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-neighbour-batch-provisions-for-jobs) for each job and can use [Amazon EC2 instances, Fargate resources](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-neighbour-batch-runs-on-ec2-fargate), so with Fargate no instance is managed.

options.text: Deploy the container image to an AWS Elastic Beanstalk environment, and start the export each day from a scheduled task in the application code.
options.why: Elastic Beanstalk is [specifically designed for running web applications](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-compute-guide-beanstalk-web-apps) on EC2 instances, so it adds instances to manage for a daily batch job.
options.misconception: uses a web application platform to run a scheduled batch job

items.explanation: Each run takes 2 to 3 hours, far longer than the [15 minutes](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-faq-timeout-15-minutes) that a Lambda function can run. Fargate runs the container with no instances to patch, and AWS Batch on Fargate also [automatically provisions compute resources](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-neighbour-batch-provisions-for-jobs) for each job.
items.takeaway: A container job that runs longer than a Lambda function can run fits Fargate or AWS Batch on Fargate.
items.twin: If the stem said "each run takes about 2 minutes" instead: a scheduled Lambda function also fits, because a function can run up to [15 minutes](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-faq-timeout-15-minutes).
items.say: A three-hour container job is too long for Lambda, so I'd run it on Fargate or on AWS Batch with Fargate.

solvers.stem_only: A 2 to 3 hour run rules out Lambda (15-minute limit) and anything that keeps servers to patch rules out EC2 and Elastic Beanstalk. Run the container serverlessly on Fargate: an ECS task started by an EventBridge schedule, or an AWS Batch job on a Fargate compute environment.

citations: docs/elasticbeanstalk/latest/dg/command-options-general#which run your application on Amazon EC2

items.stem: A company launches its application instances in us-east-1 from a launch template that uses a custom AMI. The operations team builds a new AMI each month. For cross-Region disaster recovery, the company must be able to launch identical instances in us-west-2 within 1 hour if us-east-1 becomes unavailable. The same AWS account owns all resources in both Regions. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
keywords: builds a new AMI each month

options.text: Add us-west-2 to the launch permissions of the AMI in us-east-1, so that instances in us-west-2 can launch from the same AMI.
options.why: Launch permissions [determine who can use an AMI](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-ami-launch-permissions-categories): [specific AWS accounts, organizations, or organizational units](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-ami-launch-permissions-categories), not Regions.
options.misconception: believes that AMI launch permissions can name a Region

options.text: Reference the AMI ID from us-east-1 in a launch template in us-west-2, because one AMI ID is valid in every Region.
options.why: The us-east-1 AMI ID does not exist in us-west-2, because [AMIs are Region-specific resources](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-ami-region-specific-copy).

options.text: Copy the AMI to us-west-2 after each monthly build, and reference the copied AMI in a launch template in us-west-2.
options.why: You [copy it from the source Region](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-ami-region-specific-copy) to each target Region, so a current copy waits in us-west-2 and the launch template there names it.

options.text: Write a runbook that installs and configures the application on new instances in us-west-2 when a disaster occurs.
options.why: It can work, but a manual build during a disaster is slow and error-prone, and it is more work than one AMI copy each month.

items.explanation: [AMIs are Region-specific resources](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-ami-region-specific-copy), so an instance launches from an AMI in its own Region. A copy after each monthly build keeps an identical image ready in us-west-2, and a launch template there turns the copy into instances with one call.
items.takeaway: An AMI lives in one Region, so copy it to the recovery Region before a disaster.
items.twin: If the stem said "a second AWS account in us-east-1 must launch the instances" instead: share the AMI, because launch permissions name [specific AWS accounts, organizations, or organizational units](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-ami-launch-permissions-categories).
items.say: An AMI lives in one Region, so I'd copy it to the recovery Region after every build.

solvers.stem_only: AMIs are Regional: copy each new AMI to us-west-2 after the monthly build (automate the copy) and keep a launch template in us-west-2 that references the copied AMI.

items.stem: A company runs ten Amazon EC2 Linux instances that are not in an Auto Scaling group. Each instance has 32 GiB of memory, and the instance type supports hibernation. The instances were launched from a launch template without hibernation and with unencrypted Amazon EBS root volumes. Replacing the instances is acceptable. The company now stops the instances each night and must ensure that the memory state of each instance is kept across these nightly stops. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
keywords: launched from a launch template without hibernation

options.text: Turn on hibernation for the running instances, and stop them each night with the StopInstances API and its Hibernate parameter.
options.why: Hibernation is chosen [when you launch it](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-hibernate-enable-only-at-launch); you [can't enable hibernation on an existing instance](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-hibernate-enable-only-at-launch), running or stopped.

options.text: Create a launch template version with hibernation enabled and an encrypted root volume large enough for the memory, and launch replacements from it.
options.why: The root volume is an [EBS volume](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-hibernate-root-volume-requirements) that [must be encrypted](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-hibernate-root-volume-requirements), and 32 GiB is within the Linux limit of [150 GiB](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-hibernate-ram-limits-linux-windows), so the replacements can hibernate.

options.text: Move the instances into an Auto Scaling group whose launch template enables hibernation, and hibernate the group's instances each night.
options.why: [You can't hibernate an instance](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-hibernate-not-in-auto-scaling-group) in an Auto Scaling group; the group marks the stopped instance unhealthy and can replace it.
options.misconception: believes that instances in an Auto Scaling group can hibernate

options.text: Launch ten replacement instances one at a time in the console, and turn on hibernation and root volume encryption by hand for each one.
options.why: It works, but ten manual launches are more work and more error-prone than one launch template version that every replacement uses.

items.explanation: Hibernation is a launch-time setting: you [can't enable hibernation on an existing instance](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-hibernate-enable-only-at-launch). Each replacement also needs a root volume that [must be encrypted](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-hibernate-root-volume-requirements) and has room for the memory. A new launch template version holds both settings, so the ten replacements launch the same way.
items.takeaway: Hibernation is set at launch; to add it, launch replacements from a launch template version that enables it.
items.twin: If the stem said "launched with hibernation enabled and with encrypted EBS root volumes" instead: stop them with the [StopInstances API with an additional ‘Hibernate’ parameter](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-faq-hibernate-trigger-stopinstances).
items.say: You can't add hibernation to a running instance, so launch replacements from a template that turns it on.

solvers.stem_only: Hibernation has to be set at launch, and the root EBS volume must be encrypted and big enough to hold the RAM, so the existing unencrypted instances cannot just be switched over. Make a new launch template version with hibernation on and an encrypted, large enough root volume, launch replacements from it, then hibernate them (stop with hibernate) each night.

citations: docs/AWSEC2/latest/UserGuide/hibernating-prerequisites#The root volume must be large enough to
docs/AWSEC2/latest/UserGuide/hibernating-prerequisites#You can enable hibernation support for a

solvers.flag: Neither the key nor option A says the nightly stop must change to a hibernate call, so the stem leaves open whether replacing instances alone meets the memory requirement, and A is a defensible (if higher-effort) second path.

items.stem: A company runs a batch workload that can tolerate interruption on Spot Instances. All instances use one instance type in one Availability Zone, and the request uses the lowest-price allocation strategy. Interruptions are frequent, and many jobs restart several times before they finish. The workload can run on many instance types and in any Availability Zone of the Region. The company wants fewer interruptions and wants to keep using Spot Instances. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
keywords: one instance type in one Availability Zone
can run on many instance types

options.text: Keep the lowest-price allocation strategy, because it picks the cheapest Spot capacity pools and so gives the lowest cost for the workload.
options.why: Lowest price has the [highest risk of interruption](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-fleet-spot-price-capacity-optimized-recommended), so keeping it leaves the frequent restarts in place.

options.text: Set a higher maximum Spot price in the request, so that Amazon EC2 interrupts the instances less often when the Spot price rises.
options.why: With a maximum price set, instances are [interrupted more frequently](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-spot-max-price-more-interruptions) than without one, so a higher price does not protect them.

options.text: Create separate Spot requests for several instance types in each Availability Zone, and route jobs by hand to the pools with fewer interruptions.
options.why: It spreads the jobs across more pools, but many separate requests and routing by hand are more work than one Auto Scaling group.
options.misconception: manages Spot capacity pools by hand instead of with an allocation strategy

options.text: Run the workload in an Auto Scaling group with many instance types across several Availability Zones and the price-capacity-optimized allocation strategy.
options.why: AWS recommends [price-capacity-optimized](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-spot-price-capacity-optimized-recommended), which draws from [the most-available Spot capacity pools](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-spot-price-capacity-optimized-recommended), and the group spreads many types and zones with one configuration.

items.explanation: Interruptions fall when Spot can choose from many pools. A Spot best practice is to be [flexible about which instance types you request](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-spot-be-flexible-types-and-azs) and in which Availability Zones you deploy. AWS recommends launching Spot fleets [with Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-fleet-auto-scaling-recommended-method), and price-capacity-optimized picks the most available pools at a low price.
items.takeaway: Fewer Spot interruptions come from many pools and price-capacity-optimized, not from a higher maximum price.
items.twin: If the stem said "each restart loses several hours of rendering work" instead: consider capacity-optimized, because it suits workloads with [a higher cost of interruption](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-spot-capacity-optimized-high-restart-cost).
items.say: Spread Spot across many types and zones in an Auto Scaling group, and use price-capacity-optimized.

solvers.stem_only: Diversify across many instance types and Availability Zones and use the price-capacity-optimized allocation strategy (for example in an Auto Scaling group or EC2 Fleet) so that Spot picks deeper pools.

items.stem: A company runs a license service on one Amazon EBS-backed EC2 instance. The instance is not in an Auto Scaling group and has no instance store volumes. Client applications connect to its Elastic IP address, and the license file is bound to the instance ID. The company must ensure that, after a failure of the underlying host hardware, the instance comes back with the same instance ID, private IP address, and Elastic IP address. The company wants to automate this. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
keywords: failure of the underlying host hardware
the same instance ID, private IP address, and Elastic IP address

options.text: Create an Amazon CloudWatch alarm on the system status check of the instance, and set the alarm action to recover the instance.
options.why: Recovery acts when an instance [fails a system status check](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-recovery-system-status-check-only), and the recovered instance is identical, [including the instance ID](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-recovery-keeps-id-ips-metadata) and its addresses.

options.text: Create an Amazon CloudWatch alarm on the system status check of the instance, and set the alarm action to reboot the instance.
options.why: The reboot action is [recommended for Instance Health Check failures](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-alarm-reboot-instance-check-recover-system-check), and after a reboot [the instance remains on the same host computer](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-reboot-same-host-keeps-data) that failed.
options.misconception: believes that a reboot moves an instance off failed host hardware

options.text: Register the instance with an Application Load Balancer, so that the load balancer replaces the instance when its health checks fail.
options.why: When a target fails its checks, [it stops routing traffic to that target](../facts/elb.md#elb-unhealthy-target-stop-resume); the load balancer launches no replacement and restores no instance.

options.text: Build an AWS Lambda function that stops and starts the instance, and invoke the function from an alarm on the system status check.
options.why: It can work, because you can [stop and start the instance yourself](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-status-check-system-needs-aws), but the function is custom code to maintain, and the recover action is built in.

items.explanation: Host hardware problems fail the system status check, and those problems [require AWS involvement to repair](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-status-check-system-needs-aws). The recover action is [suited for System Health Check failures](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-alarm-reboot-instance-check-recover-system-check), and a recovered instance keeps its [private IP addresses, Elastic IP addresses](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-recovery-keeps-id-ips-metadata) and instance ID. On supported types, [simplified automatic recovery is enabled during instance launch](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-recovery-simplified-enabled-by-default); of these options, the alarm is the recovery that you configure and control.
items.takeaway: A failed system status check is a host problem; the recover action keeps the instance ID and addresses.
items.twin: If the stem said "the instance status check fails because the operating system runs out of memory" instead: the reboot action, because it is [recommended for Instance Health Check failures](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-alarm-reboot-instance-check-recover-system-check).
items.say: A host failure fails the system status check, and the recover action brings back the same instance and addresses.

solvers.stem_only: Use instance recovery: a CloudWatch alarm on the system status check with the recover action; the recovered instance keeps its instance ID, private IP address and Elastic IP address.

items.stem: A company runs a data processing job on Amazon EC2 instances every night to prepare reports. The job starts at 01:00, runs for about 3 hours on four instances of the same type, and the instances are not needed for the rest of the day. The job must not be interrupted and must finish before the business day starts. Which purchasing option is the MOST cost-effective way to meet these requirements?

options.text: Launch the instances as Spot Instances each night, and terminate them after the job completes in the early morning.
options.why: [Spot Instances can be interrupted by Amazon EC2](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-spot-only-difference-interruption-two-minutes) with [two minutes of notice](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-spot-only-difference-interruption-two-minutes), and this job has to run without interruption.

options.text: Launch the instances as On-Demand Instances each night, and terminate them after the job completes in the early morning.
options.why: On-Demand Instances fit [short-term, irregular workloads that cannot be interrupted](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-on-demand-recommended-short-term-irregular), and [you pay only for the seconds](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-on-demand-billing-per-second-60s-minimum) that the instances run.

options.text: Buy Standard Reserved Instances with a 3-year term and All Upfront payment for the instance type that the job uses.
options.why: It works, but a Reserved Instance is a [one-year or three-year commitment](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-ri-term-one-or-three-years) for one configuration, and the job uses its instances for about 3 hours a night.

options.text: Launch the instances on Dedicated Hosts each night, and release the hosts after the job completes in the early morning.
options.why: Dedicated Hosts [help you address compliance requirements](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-purchasing-option-guidance) and server-bound licenses, and the stem names neither, so the hosts add cost.
options.misconception: Dedicated Hosts lower the cost of a short job

items.explanation: The job has to run without interruption, which rules out Spot. AWS recommends On-Demand Instances for [short-term, irregular workloads that cannot be interrupted](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-on-demand-recommended-short-term-irregular). A [one-year or three-year commitment](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-ri-term-one-or-three-years) suits steady use, not a job of about 3 hours a night.
items.takeaway: Work that has to finish without interruption runs on On-Demand, not Spot; a commitment pays off for steady use.
items.twin: If the stem said "The job can tolerate interruption and can restart from its last checkpoint" instead: Spot Instances, because AWS recommends Spot for [stateless, fault-tolerant, flexible applications](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-spot-recommended-stateless-fault-tolerant-flexible).
items.say: The job can't be interrupted, so I'd use On-Demand, not Spot, and skip a commitment for three hours a night.

solvers.stem_only: Short daily run of about 3 hours that must not be interrupted: On-Demand Instances launched each night and terminated after; a commitment for 24 hours would cost more, and Spot can be interrupted.

items.stem: A company runs a production web application on Amazon EC2 instances in one AWS Region. The production application must be highly available and must keep serving users if one Availability Zone fails. The company also runs a development copy of the application that engineers use only during office hours on weekdays. A short outage of the development environment is acceptable. Which combination of steps is the MOST cost-effective way to meet these requirements? (Select TWO.)
keywords: must keep serving users if one Availability Zone fails
A short outage of the development environment is acceptable

options.text: Run the production instances in two or more Availability Zones of the Region behind an Application Load Balancer.
options.why: Instances [in multiple Availability Zones](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-multi-az-protects-from-location-failure) survive [the failure of a single location](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-multi-az-protects-from-location-failure) in the Region.

options.text: Run the production instances on larger instance types in one Availability Zone behind an Application Load Balancer.
options.why: All the instances stop serving if their one zone fails, and a load balancer does not change that; production needs instances [in multiple Availability Zones](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-multi-az-protects-from-location-failure).

options.text: Run the development instances in one Availability Zone, and stop them outside office hours and on weekends.
options.why: You can [save money by deploying your resources in only one Availability Zone](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-dev-test-one-az-saves-money) for development, and turning instances off after hours saves [70% or more](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-wa-turn-off-after-hours-70-percent).

options.text: Run the development instances in three Availability Zones, and hold their capacity with On-Demand Capacity Reservations.
options.why: Development accepts an outage, so three zones add cost, and a reservation is [charged at the equivalent On-Demand rate](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-capacity-reservation-charged-used-or-not) even when nothing runs in it.

options.text: Run the production application in two AWS Regions, with active instances in both Regions at all times.
options.why: A second Region adds cost that the stem does not ask for, because instances [in multiple Availability Zones](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-multi-az-protects-from-location-failure) already survive a zone failure.

items.explanation: The two environments need different availability. Production has to survive a zone failure, so it runs [in multiple Availability Zones](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-multi-az-protects-from-location-failure) behind the load balancer. Development accepts an outage, so one zone and stops after office hours cut its cost by [70% or more](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-wa-turn-off-after-hours-70-percent).
items.takeaway: Match availability to the workload class: production in several zones, development in one zone and stopped after hours.
items.twin: If the stem said "the development environment also has to survive a zone failure" instead: run development [across multiple Availability Zones](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-bp-multi-az-critical-components) as well.
items.say: Production goes across two zones behind the load balancer; development stays in one zone and stops at night.

solvers.stem_only: Production: instances across two or more Availability Zones behind an Application Load Balancer. Development: one Availability Zone, stopped outside office hours.

items.stem: A company plans to migrate Microsoft SQL Server databases from its data center to Amazon EC2. The company owns SQL Server licenses that it is allowed to bring to AWS. The license terms count physical cores, and the vendor requires the company to report the number of sockets and physical cores that the software runs on. The databases run all day, every day. Which solution is the MOST cost-effective way to meet these requirements?
keywords: report the number of sockets and physical cores

options.text: Launch the database instances as Dedicated Instances, and bring the existing SQL Server licenses to the instances.
options.why: Dedicated Instances give [no visibility](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-dedicated-host-socket-core-visibility) of sockets and physical cores, so the company cannot report them to the vendor.

options.text: Launch the database instances on Amazon EC2 Dedicated Hosts, and bring the existing SQL Server licenses to the hosts.
options.why: Dedicated Hosts show [the number of sockets and physical cores](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-dedicated-host-socket-core-visibility) and support [per-socket, per-core, or per-VM software licenses](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-dedicated-host-byol-per-socket-core).

options.text: Launch the database instances with shared tenancy from AMIs that include the SQL Server license in the hourly price.
options.why: License-included AMIs work, but the company pays for SQL Server again, although its own licenses on Dedicated Hosts bring [no additional charge for software usage](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-dedicated-host-byol-no-software-charge).

options.text: Launch the database instances as Spot Instances with shared tenancy, and bring the existing SQL Server licenses to them.
options.why: Spot Instances do not suit workloads that are [inflexible, stateful, fault-intolerant, or tightly coupled](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-spot-not-suitable-stateful-inflexible), and shared tenancy shows no sockets or cores.

items.explanation: Licenses that count physical cores need a server whose cores the company can see. Dedicated Hosts give [comprehensive Bring Your Own License (BYOL) support](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-dedicated-host-byol-per-socket-core) and show [the number of sockets and physical cores](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-dedicated-host-socket-core-visibility). With its own SQL Server licenses, the company pays [no additional charge for software usage](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-dedicated-host-byol-no-software-charge).
items.takeaway: Licenses that count sockets or physical cores point to Dedicated Hosts, not Dedicated Instances.
items.twin: If the stem said "the company has no SQL Server licenses of its own" instead: license-included AMIs on shared tenancy fit, because there is no license to bring to a Dedicated Host.
items.say: The license counts cores, so I'd use Dedicated Hosts, which show sockets and cores.

solvers.stem_only: Bring-your-own per-core or per-socket licenses with visibility into sockets and physical cores: EC2 Dedicated Hosts.

items.stem: A company runs an internal API for its order system on one Amazon EC2 T3 instance in unlimited mode. The load is steady-state: average CPU utilization stays at about 80% all day, every day, far above the baseline of the instance. Each monthly bill includes charges for surplus CPU credits. The API must keep its current performance. Which change is the MOST cost-effective way to meet these requirements?

options.text: Keep the T3 instance in unlimited mode, because the hourly price of the instance covers CPU bursts of any length.
options.why: The hourly price covers spikes when the average stays at or below the baseline across a [rolling 24-hour period](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-burstable-unlimited-24-hour-baseline-rule); above it, AWS bills a [flat additional rate per vCPU-hour](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-burstable-unlimited-24-hour-baseline-rule).

options.text: Change the T3 instance to standard mode so that the instance stops accruing surplus credit charges each month.
options.why: In standard mode, an instance with no credits left [gradually comes down to baseline CPU utilization](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-burstable-standard-no-credits-down-to-baseline) and [cannot burst above baseline](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-burstable-standard-no-credits-down-to-baseline) until it earns more credits, so a steady load near 80% loses performance.
options.misconception: standard mode keeps the performance without paying for credits

options.text: Move the API to a general purpose M instance or a compute optimized C instance with a similar number of vCPUs.
options.why: AWS suggests that you [consider dedicated CPU instances](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-faq-burstable-sustained-high-cpu-use-m-or-c), such as M or C, when workloads [consistently require CPU usage much higher](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-faq-burstable-sustained-high-cpu-use-m-or-c) than the baseline.

options.text: Run the API on a T3 Spot Instance in unlimited mode, and launch a new Spot Instance after each interruption.
options.why: AWS recommends that you [launch your T4g or T3 Spot Instances in standard mode to avoid paying higher costs](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-burstable-spot-standard-mode-recommended), and interruptions break the steady API.
options.misconception: Spot removes the surplus credit charge

items.explanation: A steady load far above the baseline decides it. AWS suggests M or C instances when workloads [consistently require CPU usage much higher](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-faq-burstable-sustained-high-cpu-use-m-or-c) than the baseline. In unlimited mode, an average above the baseline across a [rolling 24-hour period](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-burstable-unlimited-24-hour-baseline-rule) adds a [flat additional rate per vCPU-hour](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-burstable-unlimited-24-hour-baseline-rule).
items.takeaway: Steady CPU far above the baseline belongs on M or C instances; burstable instances fit low averages with short peaks.
items.twin: If the stem said "CPU stays near 5% with short peaks each morning" instead: keep a burstable T instance, because it earns credits when it [stays below the CPU baseline](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-burstable-standard-earn-spend-credits).
items.say: It runs hot all day, so a T instance keeps paying for surplus credits. I'd move it to an M or C instance.

solvers.stem_only: Sustained CPU far above the burstable baseline: move off T3 to a fixed-performance M or C instance of similar vCPU count, which is cheaper than paying for surplus credits.

items.stem: A company runs a data processing job on Amazon EC2 instances every night to prepare reports. The job starts at 01:00, runs for about 3 hours on four instances of the same type, and the instances are not needed for the rest of the day. The job can tolerate interruption and can restart from its last checkpoint. Which purchasing option is the MOST cost-effective way to meet these requirements?

options.text: Launch the instances as Spot Instances each night, and terminate them after the job completes in the early morning.
options.why: AWS recommends Spot for [stateless, fault-tolerant, flexible applications](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-spot-recommended-stateless-fault-tolerant-flexible), and a restart from the last checkpoint makes an interruption acceptable.

options.text: Launch the instances as On-Demand Instances each night, and terminate them after the job completes in the early morning.
options.why: On-Demand Instances work, but they cost more than Spot Instances, which run at a discount of [up to 90%](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-spot-discount-up-to-90-percent) for work that can be interrupted.

options.text: Buy Standard Reserved Instances with a 3-year term and All Upfront payment for the instance type that the job uses.
options.why: A Reserved Instance is a [one-year or three-year commitment](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-ri-term-one-or-three-years) for instances that the job uses about 3 hours a night, so it costs more than Spot.
options.misconception: a long commitment is the cheapest choice for any repeating job

options.text: Launch the instances on Dedicated Hosts each night, and release the hosts after the job completes in the early morning.
options.why: Dedicated Hosts [help you address compliance requirements](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-purchasing-option-guidance) and server-bound licenses, and the stem names neither, so the hosts add cost.
options.misconception: Dedicated Hosts lower the cost of a short job

items.explanation: The job can tolerate interruption, so capacity that Amazon EC2 can take back fits. AWS recommends Spot for [stateless, fault-tolerant, flexible applications](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-spot-recommended-stateless-fault-tolerant-flexible) and for teams that are [flexible about when your applications run](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-purchasing-option-guidance). The checkpoint limits the loss to the work after the last save.
items.takeaway: A job that can restart from a checkpoint runs on Spot; a job that has to finish without interruption runs on On-Demand.
items.twin: If the stem said "The job must not be interrupted and must finish before the business day starts" instead: On-Demand Instances, because [Spot Instances can be interrupted by Amazon EC2](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-spot-only-difference-interruption-two-minutes).
items.say: The job can restart from a checkpoint, so Spot is the cheapest fit.

solvers.stem_only: Interruption-tolerant, checkpointed, short nightly run: Spot Instances launched each night.

items.stem: A company runs a nightly analytics job on a cluster of Amazon EC2 instances in one AWS Region. The nodes exchange several terabytes of data with each other during each run. The job can tolerate interruption, and a delay of one day is acceptable if an Availability Zone fails, because the cluster can be rebuilt from scratch. The nodes now run in three Availability Zones, and the data transfer charges are high. Which change is the MOST cost-effective way to meet these requirements?
keywords: exchange several terabytes of data with each other
a delay of one day is acceptable

options.text: Keep the nodes in three Availability Zones, and add nodes in each zone so that the cluster stays highly available.
options.why: Three zones keep the traffic between zones, and [charges apply for cross-Availability Zone communication](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-data-transfer-same-az-free-cross-az-charged), although the stem accepts a delay after a zone failure.

options.text: Assign an Elastic IP address to each node, and send the traffic between the nodes to the Elastic IP addresses.
options.why: Rates apply when public or Elastic IP addresses are used, in any zone, and the company is [only charged once for a given instance](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-faq-regional-transfer-charged-once): the Elastic IP addresses keep the charge.
options.misconception: traffic to Elastic IP addresses between instances is free

options.text: Move half of the nodes to a second AWS Region, and send the traffic between the two halves over the AWS network.
options.why: Traffic between Regions brings [a charge for data transfer across Regions](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-data-transfer-cross-region-charged), so splitting the cluster adds cost instead of removing it.
options.misconception: another Region avoids the charge between Availability Zones

options.text: Run all the nodes in one Availability Zone, and launch them into a cluster placement group in that zone.
options.why: Data transfer [within the same Availability Zone is free](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-data-transfer-same-az-free-cross-az-charged), and a cluster placement group gives [low network latency, high network throughput, or both](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-placement-cluster-recommended-traffic-between-instances).

items.explanation: The cost comes from traffic between zones: each instance is [charged for its data in and data out](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-faq-cross-az-transfer-charged-both-sides) when the other node sits in another zone. Data transfer [within the same Availability Zone is free](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-data-transfer-same-az-free-cross-az-charged). The stem accepts a delay of a day after a zone failure, so one zone is enough.
items.takeaway: Traffic between zones costs money; a job that accepts a zone outage can save that cost by running in one zone.
items.twin: If the stem said "the results are needed every morning, even if an Availability Zone fails" instead: keep several zones and pay for the transfer, because instances [in multiple Availability Zones](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-multi-az-protects-from-location-failure) survive a zone failure.
items.say: The job can wait a day after a zone failure, so I'd move all nodes into one zone and stop paying for cross-zone traffic.

solvers.stem_only: Remove cross-AZ data transfer: run all nodes in one Availability Zone, ideally in a cluster placement group; the accepted one-day delay covers a zone failure.

items.stem: A company runs a mission-critical order-processing application on 8 Amazon EC2 instances of one instance type in one Availability Zone of an AWS Region. The company will keep the same instance family in the same Region for at least the next 3 years. The company must ensure that capacity for all 8 instances is always available in that Availability Zone, even when demand for the instance type is high. Which purchasing approach is the MOST cost-effective way to meet these requirements?
keywords: must ensure that capacity for all 8 instances is always available

options.text: Create an On-Demand Capacity Reservation for the 8 instances in their Availability Zone with no end date, and cover it with a 3-year EC2 Instance Savings Plan.
options.why: A Capacity Reservation holds capacity [in a specific Availability Zone for any duration](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-capacity-reservation-immediate-no-term), and the EC2 Instance Savings Plan lowers the cost of that reserved usage.

options.text: Buy a Compute Savings Plan with a 3-year term and an hourly commitment that covers the full usage of all 8 instances in the Region.
options.why: [Savings Plans do not provide a capacity reservation](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-faq-savings-plans-no-capacity-reservation), so the plan lowers the bill but holds no capacity in the Availability Zone.

options.text: Buy an EC2 Instance Savings Plan with a 3-year term for the instance family in the Region, sized to cover all 8 instances.
options.why: An EC2 Instance Savings Plan is a billing discount too, and [Savings Plans do not provide a capacity reservation](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-faq-savings-plans-no-capacity-reservation) in any Availability Zone.

options.text: Create an On-Demand Capacity Reservation for the 8 instances in their Availability Zone with no end date, and pay the On-Demand rate for it with no commitment.
options.why: It holds the capacity, but a reservation is [charged at the equivalent On-Demand rate](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-capacity-reservation-charged-used-or-not), and the 3-year horizon lets a Savings Plan lower that cost.
options.misconception: pays the full On-Demand rate for reserved capacity that a Savings Plan can discount

items.explanation: Purchasing options [determine how AWS calculates your bill](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-purchasing-vs-capacity-reservation-independent); Capacity Reservations [determine whether capacity is held for you](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-purchasing-vs-capacity-reservation-independent). The stem needs held capacity in one Availability Zone for years, and [Savings Plans and Regional Reserved Instances apply](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-capacity-reservation-discount-from-sp-or-regional-ri) to a reservation with matching attributes, so a reservation plus a Savings Plan costs least.
items.takeaway: [Savings Plans do not provide a capacity reservation](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-faq-savings-plans-no-capacity-reservation); pair a Capacity Reservation, which holds capacity, with a Savings Plan, which lowers its cost.
items.twin: If the stem said "steady-state usage all day, every day, and capacity is not a concern" instead: an EC2 Instance Savings Plan, because it gives the higher discount on [a specific instance family within a Region](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-savings-plans-two-ec2-types-flexibility).
items.say: A Savings Plan lowers the bill but holds no capacity; a Capacity Reservation holds capacity, so I'd combine the two.

solvers.stem_only: Capacity in one Availability Zone is guaranteed only by a zonal reservation: an On-Demand Capacity Reservation (or a zonal Reserved Instance). Savings Plans give no capacity on their own, but they do discount Capacity Reservation usage. So reserve capacity for 8 instances in that AZ with an open-ended Capacity Reservation, and cover it with a 3-year EC2 Instance Savings Plan for the family, the deepest Savings Plan discount for a fixed family and Region.

items.stem: A company runs a reporting application on two Amazon EC2 Linux instances that are not in an Auto Scaling group. Each instance has 64 GiB of memory. After every start, the application spends 20 minutes loading data into memory before users can work. Users work only during business hours. The instances were launched with hibernation enabled and with an encrypted Amazon EBS root volume that is large enough to hold the memory. The company wants to avoid the 20-minute load each morning. Which solution is the MOST cost-effective way to meet these requirements?
keywords: spends 20 minutes loading data into memory

options.text: Stop the instances at the end of each business day, and start them again before users begin work the next morning.
options.why: A stop does not keep the loaded data, because on stop the [RAM is cleared](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-faq-hibernate-vs-stop-ram), so the 20-minute load runs again each morning.

options.text: Hibernate the instances at the end of each business day, and start them again before users begin work the next morning.
options.why: Hibernation [saves the contents from the instance memory (RAM)](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-hibernate-saves-ram-to-root-volume) to the EBS root volume, and at start [the RAM contents are reloaded](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-hibernate-saves-ram-to-root-volume), so users skip the load.

options.text: Copy the loaded data to instance store volumes each evening, stop the instances, and read the data from those volumes each morning.
options.why: A stop empties instance store volumes: on stop, [the data is erased](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-state-diff-instance-store-data), so the copied data is gone by morning.

options.text: Keep the instances running through the night, and cover their usage with a 1-year EC2 Instance Savings Plan to lower the cost.
options.why: It works, but the instances pay for every night hour; in hibernation, [you do not incur instance usage fees](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-hibernate-no-instance-fee-ebs-rates).

items.explanation: Hibernation suits applications that [take a long time to bootstrap](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-faq-hibernate-use-case-prewarm). It keeps the loaded data on the encrypted EBS root volume through the night, and the hibernated instances are [charged at standard EBS rates for storage](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-hibernate-no-instance-fee-ebs-rates), not for instance usage.
items.takeaway: To keep loaded memory through the night at low cost, hibernate an instance that was launched with hibernation enabled.
items.twin: If the stem said "the instances run in an Auto Scaling group" instead: use a warm pool that can [save the contents of your RAM](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-warm-pool-hibernated-ram), because [you can't hibernate an instance](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-hibernate-not-in-auto-scaling-group) in the group.
items.say: Hibernate them at night: the memory goes to the encrypted root volume, and you pay for storage, not for instance hours.

solvers.stem_only: Hibernate the instances (already enabled, encrypted root large enough) each evening and start them in the morning: memory is restored, no reload, and no compute charge overnight.

items.stem: A company runs an internal web application on one large general purpose Amazon EC2 instance. Over the last month, average CPU utilization was 9%. The load is spiky: on weekday mornings, short peaks reach 85% CPU for about 15 minutes, and then the load falls again. Memory use stays low all day. The company wants to reduce cost and still serve the morning peaks without slow responses. Which change is the MOST cost-effective way to meet these requirements?

options.text: Move the application to a smaller general purpose instance with enough vCPUs for the 9% average CPU utilization of the last month.
options.why: A size for the 9% average has no headroom for the 85% peaks, so responses slow down, and such a type [does not meet the performance requirements](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-compute-optimizer-under-provisioned-definition).
options.misconception: sizes an instance for its average CPU use and ignores the peaks

options.text: Move the application to a larger compute optimized instance, so that the short morning peaks use a smaller share of its available CPU.
options.why: It serves the peaks, but a larger instance pays for even more idle CPU, and [the low-cost burstable general purpose instances](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-burstable-low-utilization-waste-use-t) fit a low average better.

options.text: Move the application to a memory optimized instance of a smaller size, because low CPU use shows that memory limits the application.
options.why: Memory use is low, so this family solves a problem that the stem does not have: it is built to [process large data sets in memory](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-family-memory-optimized).
options.misconception: reads low CPU use as a sign that memory is the bottleneck

options.text: Move the application to a burstable T instance with the same vCPU count, so that idle hours earn CPU credits for the peaks.
options.why: The T instance earns credits while it [stays below the CPU baseline](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-burstable-standard-earn-spend-credits), and it [spends credits when it bursts above the baseline](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-burstable-standard-earn-spend-credits) in the morning peaks.

items.explanation: A low average with short peaks is the burstable pattern. When CPU use is low, a fixed instance pays for idle cycles, and AWS points to [the low-cost burstable general purpose instances](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-burstable-low-utilization-waste-use-t). The T instance banks credits in quiet hours and spends them in the peaks.
items.takeaway: A low average with short CPU peaks fits a burstable T instance; steady high CPU fits M or C.
items.twin: If the stem said "CPU stays near 80% all day" instead: an M or C instance, because AWS suggests them when workloads [consistently require CPU usage much higher](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-faq-burstable-sustained-high-cpu-use-m-or-c) than the baseline.
items.say: Low average CPU with short peaks: a burstable T instance banks credits when idle and spends them in the peaks.

steps: I read the last sentence first: it asks for the change that is the MOST cost-effective way to meet the requirements.
I mark the constraints: average CPU utilization is 9%, short morning peaks reach 85%, memory use stays low, and the peaks must not slow down.
Before I look at the options, I predict a burstable T instance, because a low average with short peaks is the pattern that CPU credits are made for.
I remove the memory optimized instance, because memory is not the limit. I remove the smaller general purpose instance, because a size for the 9% average has no room for the 85% peaks.

Between the burstable T instance and the larger compute optimized instance the difference is cost; the stem says the peaks are short and the average is low, so the T instance earns credits in idle hours and spends them in the peaks, and the larger instance pays for idle CPU.
Check: the burstable T instance keeps the same vCPU count, serves the peaks with credits, and costs less than the large fixed instance. Time: 90 seconds.

solvers.stem_only: Low average CPU with short peaks: a burstable T instance that earns CPU credits while idle and spends them during the morning peaks.

items.stem: A company runs a Python web service and a small helper program written in C on x86-based Amazon EC2 instances. The company wants to migrate the service to AWS Graviton-based instances for better price performance, with minimal code changes. The Python code does not rely on native CPU instruction sets. The instances are launched from a launch template that references an x86 AMI. Which approach will meet these requirements with the LEAST development effort?
keywords: does not rely on native CPU instruction sets

options.text: Stop the instances, change their instance type to a Graviton type of the same size, and start them again with the current AMI.
options.why: A resized instance needs [the same processor architecture](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-resize-same-processor-architecture), because [AMIs are specific to the architecture](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-resize-same-processor-architecture), so the x86 AMI cannot run on Graviton.
options.misconception: believes that an x86 AMI starts on a Graviton instance type

options.text: Build an arm64 AMI with the Python service, recompile the C helper for Arm, and update the launch template to a Graviton type.
options.why: Compiled programs [need to be re-compiled to generate Arm binaries](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-graviton-compiled-apps-recompile), and the new type needs a matching AMI, because [AMIs are specific to the architecture](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-resize-same-processor-architecture).

options.text: Rewrite the Python service in a compiled language such as Go, and build Arm binaries for both the service and the helper program.
options.why: It works, but rewriting working Python code is far more effort than recompiling one small C helper, which breaks the qualifier.

options.text: Turn on nested virtualization on the Graviton instances, and run the current x86 AMI inside a hypervisor on each instance.
options.why: Nested virtualization runs hypervisors [inside virtualized Amazon EC2 instances](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-change-nested-virtualization-2026-02); it does not change the processor, so the x86 AMI still does not fit.

items.explanation: Python code that does not rely on native CPU instruction sets moves to Arm with minimal changes. The C helper is compiled code, and on Graviton (Arm) instances compiled programs [need to be re-compiled to generate Arm binaries](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-graviton-compiled-apps-recompile). The new launch template version then names an arm64 AMI and a Graviton type, and nothing else in the service changes.
items.takeaway: Moving to Graviton needs an arm64 AMI and a recompile of compiled code; interpreted code moves with few changes.
items.twin: If the stem said "the whole service is a compiled C++ program" instead: recompile all of the code, because C++ programs [need to be re-compiled to generate Arm binaries](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-graviton-compiled-apps-recompile).
items.say: For Graviton, build an arm64 AMI and recompile the C part; the Python code moves almost unchanged.

solvers.stem_only: Build an arm64 AMI: the interpreted Python runs as is, recompile the C helper for Arm, and point the launch template at the arm64 AMI and a Graviton instance type.

items.stem: A company runs a mission-critical order-processing application on 8 Amazon EC2 instances of one instance type in one Availability Zone of an AWS Region. The company will keep the same instance family in the same Region for at least the next 3 years. The instances have steady-state usage all day, every day, and capacity is not a concern for the company. Which purchasing approach is the MOST cost-effective way to meet these requirements?
keywords: steady-state usage all day, every day
same instance family in the same Region

options.text: Create an On-Demand Capacity Reservation for 8 instances of the instance type in the Availability Zone where the instances run, with no end date.
options.why: It works, but a reservation is [charged at the equivalent On-Demand rate](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-capacity-reservation-charged-used-or-not), so it adds no discount for steady usage.
options.misconception: treats a Capacity Reservation as a discount

options.text: Buy a Compute Savings Plan with a 3-year term and an hourly commitment that covers the usage of the 8 instances in the Region.
options.why: It works, but Compute Savings Plans apply [regardless of Region, instance family, operating system](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-savings-plans-two-ec2-types-flexibility), and the company pays for that flexibility with a lower discount.

options.text: Buy an EC2 Instance Savings Plan with a 3-year term for the instance family in the Region, sized for the 8 instances.
options.why: An EC2 Instance Savings Plan covers [a specific instance family within a Region](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-savings-plans-two-ec2-types-flexibility) and gives the higher discount, which matches the fixed plan of the company.

options.text: Allocate Dedicated Hosts in the Availability Zone where the instances run, with enough capacity for the 8 instances, and launch the instances on the hosts.
options.why: It works, but each host is billed [regardless of the quantity or the size](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-dedicated-host-billed-per-host-per-second) of its instances, which adds cost without a stated isolation need.
options.misconception: pays for whole physical hosts when shared tenancy meets every requirement

items.explanation: The usage is steady, and the family and Region stay fixed, so the plan with the higher discount wins. Steady workloads [benefit most from long-term commitments through Savings Plans](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-steady-state-savings-plans), and EC2 Instance Savings Plans trade the flexibility of Compute Savings Plans for a higher discount on [a specific instance family within a Region](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-savings-plans-two-ec2-types-flexibility).
items.takeaway: For steady usage in one family and Region, an EC2 Instance Savings Plan gives the larger Savings Plans discount.
items.twin: If the stem said "capacity for all 8 instances must always be available in that Availability Zone" instead: add a Capacity Reservation, and keep the plan, because [Savings Plans and Regional Reserved Instances apply](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-capacity-reservation-discount-from-sp-or-regional-ri) to it.
items.say: Steady use, same family, same Region: an EC2 Instance Savings Plan gives the bigger discount.

solvers.stem_only: Steady usage, fixed instance family and Region for 3 years, no capacity need: an EC2 Instance Savings Plan (3-year) gives the largest discount among Savings Plans; no capacity reservation needed.
